articles.body: Europe Tankers Transocean expands newbuild programme with tanker duo Adis Ajdin October 26, 2026 0 0 1 minute read GSI GSI Monaco-based Transocean Maritime Agencies has ordered two 50,000 dwt chemical and product tankers at China’s Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI), adding another vessel type to its expanding newbuilding programme. The CSSC-controlled yard recently signed the contract, marking its first order from a Monaco-based shipowner. Financial terms, delivery dates and propulsion specifications have not been disclosed. Transocean is a family-controlled shipping company established in the 1960s by the late Guenther Neunhoeffer. The company, led by Ruth McLoughlin, operates a fleet of around 15 vessels, primarily comprising bulk carriers and tankers. The latest order follows its move into the containership market last year. In October 2025, the Monaco owner emerged as the buyer behind two-plus-two 1,930 teu feeder newbuildings at Guangzhou Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding, scheduled for delivery in 2028. The vessels, named Ajax C and Apollo C, marked Transocean’s first entry into the container segment. Shipbuilding sources have also linked the company to another two 3,100 teu containerships at New Dayang Shipbuilding. Transocean previously ordered two 64,000 dwt ultramax bulkers at New Dayang in 2024, continuing a fleet expansion strategy spanning several Chinese yards. The latest contract adds to a busy period for GSI in the MR tanker segment. The Guangzhou yard has recently attracted orders from Geneva-based Advantage Tankers and Greek owner Top Ships. articles.title: WEL Companies integrates Descartes and CARRIER1 to streamline freight operations
articles.summary: US-based transportation and logistics provider WEL Companies has integrated Descartes Systems Group’s transportation management system (TMS) with CARRIER1 Vault to streamline freight brokerage operations and improve communication across its trucking network. Announced on October 22, 2026, the integrated solution...
articles.body: US-based transportation and logistics provider WEL Companies has integrated Descartes Systems Group’s transportation management system (TMS) with CARRIER1 Vault to streamline freight brokerage operations and improve communication across its trucking network. Announced on October 22, 2026, the integrated solution enables WEL Companies to manage shipments transported by its own fleet alongside freight handled by third-party carriers within its for-hire network. The system connects brokerage activities with carrier and driver workflows, allowing shipment information, status updates and delivery documentation to move between the two platforms without requiring freight brokers to leave their existing TMS environment. “The Descartes and CARRIER1 collaboration lets WEL automate communication and shipment data across our brokerage, our assets, and our for-hire carrier network, without our brokers ever leaving their TMS,” said Eric Lenze, EVP at WEL Companies. “That means a faster shipment lifecycle and a better experience for our customers,” he added. Connecting freight brokerage and carrier operations Descartes’ cloud-based broker TMS supports key transportation management activities, including order entry, load coverage, carrier acceptance, dispatching and carrier communications. Through its integration with CARRIER1 Vault, the platform extends these capabilities to carriers and drivers, supporting digital freight tendering, shipment tracking and document exchange. As shipments progress, information such as carrier assignments, driver and equipment details, delivery status updates and transport documents can be transferred directly into the corresponding shipment records within Descartes’ system. These documents include rate confirmations, bills of lading and proof of delivery, helping brokers maintain access to shipment information through a centralised platform. The integration also supports carrier, driver and equipment verification, while reducing reliance on manual data entry and information collected through emails, spreadsheets and telephone calls. “Connecting Vault with Descartes’ TMS brings the broker, carrier and driver into the same flow of information,” said Travis Rhyan, CEO of CARRIER1. “The broker stays in their Descartes solution, the carrier gets what they need to move the load, and the information comes back without someone having to chase it down manually,” he explained. Supporting more efficient shipment management The implementation reflects efforts to improve coordination between freight brokerage teams and the carriers responsible for transporting goods. By connecting shipment management, carrier communications and document processing, WEL Companies aims to simplify administrative workflows while improving the availability of operational information throughout the shipment lifecycle. Andrew Wimer, Associate General Manager at Descartes, said the integration enables brokers to access specialised capabilities while retaining the company’s TMS as their central operating platform. According to Wimer, extending the system to carriers and drivers allows brokerage teams to spend less time collecting shipment updates and documentation and more time managing operational exceptions and customer requirements. The companies did not disclose financial terms or provide quantified performance results from the implementation.

articles.body: Asia Containers Transworld gets green light for $43m boxship deal Adis Ajdin October 26, 2026 0 15 1 minute read Transworld Transworld India’s Transworld Shipping Lines has secured shareholder approval for the $42.78m acquisition of two containerships from another company within its controlling shareholder’s group, clearing a key hurdle in its ongoing fleet restructuring. The Navi Mumbai-based listed owner disclosed in a filing that shareholders had backed the purchase of the 2006-built OEL Surya and OEL Varun from Orient Express Lines Inc. The transaction will be carried out through Transworld Sea-Connect IFSC, a wholly owned subsidiary of the shipping company. The 2,748 teu OEL Surya is valued at $22.03m, while the 2,478 teu OEL Varun carries a price tag of $20.75m. Both acquisitions were originally approved by Transworld’s board on September 7, subject to shareholder consent and any other necessary approvals. The two vessels are already commercially employed, providing Transworld with an existing income stream as it brings the tonnage onto its subsidiary’s books. The move follows a series of disposals and acquisitions as Transworld reshapes its vessel portfolio. Earlier this month, the company agreed to acquire the 2011-built, 55,648 dwt supramax Saltwind Explorer for $16.5m.In September, it struck a $9.25m deal to sell the 2011-built bulker TBC Kailash to Mandarine Ocean, following several containership disposals to DP World-controlled Avana Logistek. Transworld retained its shipowning and dry bulk businesses when DP World’s Unifeeder acquired the group’s Indian coastal and feeder operations in a transaction completed in 2021. The latest purchases represent a transfer of existing tonnage between related entities, rather than an addition to the wider controlling group’s combined fleet. The same data builds the evidence needed to demonstrate compliance with UK, EU and international environmental standards. articles.body: Middle East Shipyards Tankers Bahri turns to homegrown yard for $451m VLCC trio Adis Ajdin October 26, 2026 0 88 1 minute read Bahri Bahri Saudi shipping giant Bahri has ordered three very large crude carriers at International Maritime Industries (IMI), committing SAR1.692bn ($451m) to expand its tanker fleet and support shipbuilding at home. The 320,000 dwt vessels will be built at IMI’s Ras Al Khair facility on Saudi Arabia’s eastern coast, with deliveries scheduled between 2029 and 2030. The contract, signed on October 22 and disclosed on Sunday, works out at approximately $150m per ship. Bahri said the newbuildings would feature advanced energy-efficiency technologies and be financed through a combination of internal cash and bank facilities. The Riyadh-listed owner holds a 19.9% stake in IMI, a joint venture with Saudi Aramco, South Korea’s HD Hyundai and Lamprell. Bahri chief executive Ahmed Al-Subaey also sits on the shipbuilder’s board. The latest agreement takes Bahri’s Saudi newbuilding commitments to nine vessels, following a $203m order for six geared ultramax bulk carriers at the same yard in October last year. Those 62,823 dwt ships are scheduled for delivery between 2028 and 2029 and marked the launch of Saudi Arabia’s first large-scale commercial shipbuilding programme. IMI has already been involved in Bahri’s VLCC fleet development. In 2021, the owner took delivery of the 319,000 dwt Rayah, built under an earlier IMI and Hyundai Heavy Industries partnership. That vessel was constructed in South Korea, with Saudi engineers participating in the project as part of a technology transfer arrangement. The new order also adds to Bahri’s wider tanker fleet renewal drive. The company completed a $1bn acquisition of nine modern VLCCs from Evangelos Marinakis-controlled Capital Maritime & Trading last year, following a string of secondhand tanker purchases. Earlier this year, Bahri added five chemical tankers and disposed of an older VLCC, taking its owned fleet to 107 vessels at the end of June. The Saudi group has been building up its fleet across several sectors, including an ongoing programme of conro newbuildings, while its crude tanker business remains a key part of its operations. articles.summary: LNG The LNG market showed some signs of recovery this week, with increased fixing activity absorbing some of the available tonnage across both basins. articles.body: LNG Shipping Market Recovering in International Shipping News 26/10/2026 LNG The LNG market showed some signs of recovery this week, with increased fixing activity absorbing some of the available tonnage across both basins. Despite this, competition for cargoes remains high and charterers continue to hold negotiating leverage, limiting the extent of upward movement in spot rates. On the BLNG1 Australia–Japan route, rates increased by $4,800 week-on-week to settle at $32,800/day. The Pacific market firmed gradually as vessel availability tightened slightly and several late November and early December requirements emerged. The BLNG2 US Gulf–Continent route increased by $4,000 to close at $25,400/day. Increased fixing activity helped absorb some of the available Atlantic tonnage, although continued competition between owners kept the recovery in rates measured. Similarly, the BLNG3 US Gulf–Japan route gained $10,300 week-on-week to settle at $58,900/day. Eastbound cargoes continue to command a premium, although limited arbitrage economics are restricting further upside. In the time charter market, sentiment was mixed. The six-month rate fell by $1,800 to $40,700/day, while the one-year term increased by $700 to $51,800/day. Further out the curve, the three-year period rose by $600 to $70,500/day. LPG The LPG market softened this week as the arbitrage narrowed and the position list lengthened slightly. With more tonnage becoming available, charterers regained some negotiating leverage, although vessel supply remains broadly balanced and sentiment remains firm. On the BLPG1 Ras Tanura–Chiba route, rates settled at $252.40/tonne, with TCE earnings closing at $242,380/day. The BLPG2 Houston–Flushing route declined by $11.33 week-on-week to settle at $171.67/tonne, with TCE earnings falling by $17,332 to $197,244/day. The softer arbitrage and slight increase in vessel availability weighed on rates through the week. Similarly, the BLPG3 Houston–Chiba route fell $29.14 to close at $305.71/tonne, while TCE returns decreased by $24,396 to $181,218/day. The route saw the larger correction as eastbound economics softened, and charterers gained some negotiating leverage. Source: Baltic Exchange 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: USTR proposes extending port fee suspension on China-linked ships to January
articles.summary: The US Trade Representative proposed extending the suspension of port fees on Chinese-linked ships for an additional two months, delaying higher shipping costs for US metals and coal exporters, according to a Federal Register public inspection document posted late last week. USTR had suspended a fee targeting China’s...
articles.body: USTR proposes extending port fee suspension on China-linked ships to January in International Shipping News 26/10/2026 The US Trade Representative proposed extending the suspension of port fees on Chinese-linked ships for an additional two months, delaying higher shipping costs for US metals and coal exporters, according to a Federal Register public inspection document posted late last week. USTR had suspended a fee targeting China’s maritime, logistics and shipping sectors for one year, through Nov. 9, 2026, as part of a US-China trade deal. USTR is proposing to extend the suspension through Jan. 9, 2027. Platts first reported the likely extension on Oct. 20. “The United States is continuing to engage with China with the goal of obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices at issue in the investigation. The Trade Representative is therefore proposing to further suspend for two months, through January 9, 2027, the responsive actions taken in this investigation,” said the public inspection document, scheduled to be published in the Federal Register Oct. 26. Platts is part of S&P Global Energy. The proposed punt follows a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in September. The two leaders are expected to meet again in November. The suspended port fees include a fee on vessels owned or operated by Chinese entities and a separate fee on Chinese-built vessels. The initial rates were $50/net ton per voyage for Chinese-owned or operated vessels and $18/nt or $120 per container discharged for Chinese-built vessels. Net tons are equivalent to short tons. The revised fees are less stringent than USTR’s initial proposal, which would have charged up to $1.5 million per entrance of Chinese-built vessels. When first announced in early 2025, the fee proposal caused alarm in the coal industry, which relies on exports amid declining domestic consumption and has few alternatives to Chinese-built ships. The National Coal Council has recommended that the Trump administration make the suspension of the port fees permanent, according to a July 2026 report on US coal exports. The maritime actions would raise costs for transportation, reduce vessel availability and undermine the competitiveness of US coal exports, the council said. USTR is seeking comments on the proposed two-month extension. Comments are due Oct. 30. Source: Platts 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: From Dark Voyages to Defensible Claims: How Marine Insurers Are Closing the Evidence Gap
articles.summary: Claims teams in marine insurance own two things: the loss investigation and the pay-or-reject decision. In the pre-2022 environment, both were largely a matter of establishing what happened, verifying that the loss fell within the policy’s coverage, and processing accordingly. AIS records, cargo documentation, and...
articles.body: From Dark Voyages to Defensible Claims: How Marine Insurers Are Closing the Evidence Gap in International Shipping News , Marine Insurance P&I Club News 26/10/2026 Claims teams in marine insurance own two things: the loss investigation and the pay-or-reject decision. In the pre-2022 environment, both were largely a matter of establishing what happened, verifying that the loss fell within the policy’s coverage, and processing accordingly. AIS records, cargo documentation, and standard loss adjustment supported the investigation without requiring extensive forensic reconstruction. In 2026, that has shifted. Claims investigations increasingly begin with the question of what actually happened during a defined period, because the AIS record from that period may not answer it reliably. Vessels operating in jamming-affected regions may have broadcast injected coordinates rather than actual positions. Vessels that were dark did not broadcast at all. Reconstructing the actual voyage is the analytical work claims teams now do before the pay-or-reject decision becomes possible. Four operational realities define the environment. 1. The AIS Reliability Problem at Claims The historical premise of AIS-based loss investigation is that AIS records reflect what vessels actually did. That premise has been under pressure since 2022 and has become materially unreliable in 2026 for specific regions and activity types. Windward’s Q3 2026 Maritime Risk Report tracked 124,235 vessels affected by GPS jamming at least once globally, with jamming running at an average of 5,131 incidents per day across the quarter, broadly unchanged from Q2. Since Operation Epic Fury began in February 2026, Windward has recorded more than 3.35 million false ship-to-ship meetings, in which injected positioning coordinates made vessels appear to rendezvous when no meeting took place. Jamming is persistent in the Middle East Gulf, the Black Sea, the Mediterranean, and other high-exposure regions, which are exactly where marine insurance claims from the current environment concentrate. For a claims team investigating a loss involving a vessel that operated in a jamming-affected region during the relevant period, the AIS record includes potentially injected coordinates, potentially missing intervals, and potentially false event records. A vessel that appears to have transited a specific route may have taken a different one. A vessel that appears to have made no port calls may have made calls the AIS record does not show. The compliance evidence base that claims rely on to establish whether the vessel was engaged in sanctionable activity at the time of loss depends on this AIS record being accurate. When it is not, the compliance evidence base becomes vulnerable to challenge. When the evidence base is vulnerable, the claims decision made against it is also vulnerable. 2. The Hormuz Stranded Vessel Environment The operational environment produced by the Hormuz closure earlier in 2026 has created a distinct claims scenario many teams are still working through. Following the outbreak of the Iran conflict on February 28, 2026, and Operation Epic Fury the same day, vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz collapsed. February recorded approximately 3,750 AIS-visible monthly transits. March fell to 450. Even after a partial recovery, June remained approximately 83% below pre-conflict baselines. Traffic briefly rebounded following the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding between Iran and the U.S. and the formal lifting of the blockade on June 18, before Iran reimposed closure on June 20 and reinstated the Persian Gulf Strait Authority toll and clearance system. Traffic has not recovered since. Windward counted 55 AIS-visible transits between September 16 and 23, approximately 94% below pre-war levels, and attacks on shipping in the corridor continued through the quarter. For claims teams, the Hormuz situation has generated several specific claim types. Constructive Total Loss Questions Many war risk clauses set a 12-month detention period before a constructive total loss can be declared, with some policies operating on a 6-month period. Vessels stranded during the closure raise the question of whether extended detention in the Middle East Gulf may qualify for constructive total loss even without sustaining physical damage. Investigating these claims requires establishing the specific detention timeline, the operational conditions during the detention, and whether the vessel is genuinely constructively total loss or eventually recoverable. Loss Of Hire Claims Vessels unable to complete voyages during the closure have generated loss of hire claims, though not every loss of hire policy responds without physical loss or damage. Claims teams are working through the specific policy language and operational circumstances that determine whether coverage applies. Dark Period Disputes Many vessels transiting the Hormuz war-risk zone did so with AIS switched off, in some cases with owner and flag state consent for safety and security reasons. This is now the majority practice rather than the exception. Windward estimates that dark convoy passages accounted for 47% of Hormuz traffic in August 2026 and 52% in September. When a loss occurred during a dark period, or when the vessel’s activity during a dark period is contested by the charterer, cargo interest, or insurer, the investigation depends on reconstructing what happened during a window when the vessel was not self-reporting. Each of these claim types requires forensic work that goes beyond AIS records. 3. The Legal Environment Is Calibrating The English Court of Appeal ruling in Tonzip Maritime (Singapore) Pte Ltd v 2 Rivers Pte Ltd, The CATALAN SEA, handed down on May 22, 2026, clarified how courts are approaching contested contractual terms in the current environment. The Court held that the threshold for invoking sanctions clauses is a reasonable judgment of a real risk of sanctions, not proof that a breach would probably occur. The case is a charterparty dispute, not directly an insurance case, but the ruling has implications for how sanctions clauses in insurance policies will be interpreted. The lower evidential threshold gives insurers, owners, and their counterparties more flexibility to invoke sanctions clauses to decline coverage, refuse claims, or terminate policies. It also raises the standard for the underlying evidential basis. A sanctions clause invoked under the “reasonable judgment of real risk” threshold still requires evidence sufficient to support that judgment. For claims teams, this means the evidence base supporting a claims decision, particularly a decision to decline a claim on sanctions-related grounds, needs to be defensible in a legal environment actively calibrating the standards. A claims decision made on AIS position data from a jamming-affected region may be vulnerable to challenge if the AIS record itself is not defensible. A claims decision made on multi-sensor reconstruction that verifies actual vessel activity is materially more defensible. The OFAC-OFSI Comparative Overview published on June 23, 2026 documents the differences between U.S. and UK sanctions frameworks across ownership calculations, terminology, jurisdictional reach, and enforcement mechanics. Claims teams operating across multiple sanctions regimes need to structure their evidence base to satisfy the more demanding standard in each regime. Both OFAC and OFSI apply strict liability for civil penalties, meaning claims decisions that inadvertently touch sanctioned activity can create enforcement exposure even without knowledge that the transaction was prohibited. 4. What Forensic Reconstruction Actually Requires Reconstructing vessel activity during a contested period is an all-source intelligence exercise. It draws on whatever independent evidence exists for that vessel in that window, selected for what the specific question requires rather than from a fixed list of feeds. What those sources have in common is that none of them depends on the vessel’s own broadcasts. Satellite Imagery Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) provides vessel detection regardless of weather and lighting conditions, capable of confirming vessel presence at specific locations when AIS is off or unreliable. Electro-optical (EO) imagery provides visual confirmation of vessel activity, including ship-to-ship transfers, port calls, and vessel proximity to other assets. High-resolution EO can capture visual detail down to 30 centimeters, supporting vessel identification through distinguishing features. Radio Frequency (RF) Detection Vessels emit RF signals from their operational systems even when AIS is off. RF detection provides an independent positioning signal that can confirm or contradict a vessel’s stated location during a period when it was not broadcasting AIS. Documentary and Commercial Records Terminal and berth records, charter documentation, cargo and customs paperwork, class and registry entries, and port state control inspection histories establish what was declared, by whom, and when. None of this is sensor data, and none of it arrives as a feed. It is often the most direct evidence available of what a vessel was contracted to do during the period in question, and in a dispute it is the material counsel will reach for first. Behavioral Pattern Analysis A vessel’s operational history across multiple voyages, ownership profile, flag history, and comparative behavior against similar vessels of similar type provide analytical context. A vessel that has gone dark in circumstances consistent with a legitimate historical operational pattern carries different risk than a vessel that has gone dark in an anomalous manner. All-Source Intelligence Fusion When these sources are combined, they produce a reconstructed picture of what the vessel actually did during the contested period, with the specific evidence supporting each conclusion identified and weighted. Those four evidence types are the ones that come up most often. They are not the limit. A reconstruction reaches for whatever evidence exists for that vessel in that window, and what exists varies case by case: device presence signals in a remote anchorage, camera identification at a chokepoint transit, a bunkering record, an inspection report, the insured party’s own voyage documentation. Any of them can be the piece that settles the question. This means that the evidence a case needs is rarely known before the case opens. A reconstruction built only from sources that happen to be connected in advance will answer the question those sources can answer, and go quiet on the one that matters. Imagery changes what can be settled rather than argued. A SAR detection placing a vessel at a specific position at a specific time is not an inference drawn from a gap in the record. It is an observation, and it closes questions that previously stayed open through an entire dispute. A reconstruction will not produce certainty on every point. What it produces is a step-by-step, timestamped account of the contested period, with the evidence behind each step identified and a stated level of confidence attached to it. Some steps are confirmed by direct observation. Others are assessed from behavior and context, and are presented that way. That is what makes a decision defensible. Not that every question was answered, but that the basis for each conclusion is documented, weighted, and available for counsel, arbitrators, or regulators to examine. How Windward Supports Marine Insurance Claims Teams Windward’s all-source operational intelligence platform delivers the reconstruction that claims investigations increasingly require. It fuses AIS with satellite imagery, RF detection, ownership records, sanctions data, behavioral history, and whatever else the case calls for, including documentation the claims team already holds, into a single operational picture. The result establishes what a vessel actually did during a defined period, independently of what it broadcast, and gives the file a defensible evidence base for whether the vessel was engaged in sanctionable or non-compliant activity at the time of loss. Claims teams with internal analytical capacity use it directly, running the reconstruction against the specific facts of the case in front of them. Where a case requires expert-led investigation, the Maritime Intelligence Operations Center (MIOC) provides analyst services on behalf of the claims team. Windward’s maritime intelligence experts conduct the dark period reconstruction, apply the analytical methodology to the specific facts of the case, and produce a documented report suitable for legal or arbitration proceedings. Each MIOC report details the analytical approach, the sensor inputs relied on, the evidential basis for every finding, and the confidence level assigned to each conclusion. For claims teams handling Hormuz-related constructive total loss questions, loss of hire claims, dark period disputes, or standard cargo and hull claims involving vessels that operated in jamming-affected regions, the operational fit is direct. Where This Is Heading The environment that has emerged across 2026 is not returning to the pre-2022 baseline. GPS jamming has plateaued rather than receded, holding at roughly 5,131 incidents per day through Q3, and will continue while the Iran conflict remains unresolved. Vessels stranded during the Hormuz closure will continue to produce constructive total loss and loss of hire claims. Dark period disputes will continue as long as vessels transit war-risk zones with AIS switched off. Sanctions-related claims decisions will continue to be tested against evolving case law and enforcement standards. Claims teams who have adapted their investigation methodology to include multi-sensor forensic reconstruction are producing defensible decisions in this environment. Claims teams still relying on AIS records alone are producing decisions that may not hold up under legal or regulatory review. The gap between the two is measurable in claim defensibility, litigation exposure, and reserving accuracy. It will continue to widen. Source: Windward 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: In the pre-2022 environment, both were largely a matter of establishing what happened, verifying that the loss fell within the policy’s coverage, and processing accordingly.
AIS records, cargo documentation, and standard loss adjustment supported the investigation without requiring extensive forensic reconstruction.
Claims investigations increasingly begin with the question of what actually happened during a defined period, because the AIS record from that period may not answer it reliably.

articles.title: Pilot transfer operation: A safer step aboard
articles.summary: Safe pilot transfer operations depend on both correct procedures and fit-for-purpose equipment. articles.body: Pilot transfer operation: A safer step aboard in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 26/10/2026 Safe pilot transfer operations depend on both correct procedures and fit-for-purpose equipment. New SOLAS requirements entering into force in 2028 will introduce mandatory performance standards for pilot transfer arrangements, and some existing installations may require physical modifications. Ship operators should start a fleet-wide review of their arrangements now. Pilot ladders remain a recurring safety concern Successive safety campaigns by the International Maritime Pilots’ Association (IMPA) provide a useful picture of the scale and nature of non-compliant pilot transfer arrangements. The 2026 campaign recorded 4,051 observations from pilots across 34 countries, with an overall non-compliance rate of 13%. While this represents a slight improvement from the previous year, IMPA reports no significant change to historic non-compliance trends. More than half of the non-compliances concerned the pilot ladder itself, with access to the deck, safety equipment and combination arrangements also recurring areas of concern. Common defects included incorrectly rigged retrieval lines, ladders not secured to strong points and missing lifebuoys. Port State control findings tell a similar story. In its August 2025 safety bulletin, the Tokyo MOU reported that deficiencies related to pilot transfer arrangements increased from 197 in 2020 to 523 in 2024, with associated detentions rising from one to 12. Recurring issues included failure to properly secure pilot and accommodation ladders to the ship’s side, inadequate securing of stanchions with locking pins, complacency regarding ladder maintenance, and a lack of clear identification and differentiation between pilot ladders and other types of ladders. When things go wrong Accidents associated with pilot transfer arrangements have resulted in fatalities and serious injuries, and the risks are not limited to the pilots using them. Crew members responsible for preparing and rigging the arrangements can also be exposed to serious hazards. The UK’s Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) has investigated many incidents involving falls and injuries associated with pilot transfer operations. In one such case, a pilot fell approximately three metres onto a pilot boat and suffered a fractured ankle after losing their grip on a handhold stanchion. MAIB’s preliminary assessment found that the stanchions were not fit for purpose, as their design prevented the pilot from gaining a firm grip when reaching the top of the ladder. The examples below, taken from the MAIB Annual Report 2022, show non-compliant handhold stanchions at the transition from the pilot ladder to the deck. More recently, in October 2025, the bosun of a bulk carrier died after falling overboard while the crew was preparing the pilot ladder. The MAIB investigation found that the pilot ladder davit was not fit for use and that the crew had become accustomed to manually lowering and recovering the ladder close to an unguarded deck edge. This unsafe practice had become normalised, placing the crew at serious risk. Crew members working in the area were also not equipped with appropriate personal protective equipment to prevent a fall, arrest a fall or support them in the water. New requirements from 2028 In June 2025, IMO adopted revised SOLAS Regulation V/23 and new mandatory Performance Standards for Pilot Transfer Arrangements (MSC.572(110) and MSC.576(110)), entering into force on 1 January 2028. The standards address the design, installation, maintenance and safe use of pilot transfer arrangements and also apply to existing arrangements. The important timeline is as follows: • New installations: Pilot transfer arrangements installed on or after 1 January 2028 must meet the new requirements for design, manufacture, construction, securing, and installation (Parts A, B and C of MSC.576(110)). • Existing installations: Arrangements installed before 1 January 2028 must meet the same requirements by the first survey on or after 1 January 2029 for SOLAS ships and 1 January 2030 for non-SOLAS ships. • All installations: Requirements for inspection, stowage, maintenance, replacement, and familiarisation apply from 1 January 2028, regardless of installation date (Introduction and Parts D and E of MSC.576(110)). Compliance may require physical modifications to existing pilot transfer arrangements. Examples include more detailed provisions for the strength, marking and documentation of strong points used for securing ladders and manropes. More specific provisions also apply to access to deck, including the dimensions, positioning and securing of handholds and stanchions. Combination arrangements using an accommodation ladder are also subject to more detailed requirements, including for trapdoor openings, the positioning of the pilot ladder and the provision of handholds. Older accommodation ladder arrangements, particularly those dating from before the 2012 SOLAS amendments, may require more extensive modifications. For further details on the changes and their implementation, see the technical bulletins available on the websites of classification societies, including DNV, Lloyd’s Register, ABS, and ClassNK. For practical guidance, IMO circular MSC.1/Circ.1428/Rev.1 provides updated illustrations of pilot transfer arrangements compliant with the new performance standards. The illustrations are also available to download via the IMPA resource page. What should ship operators do now? Ship operators should start preparing early. Key actions include: • Assessing existing pilot transfer arrangements against the new requirements to identify any compliance gaps. • Planning necessary modifications, particularly where engineering work or structural alterations may be required, and considering whether these can be coordinated with already scheduled repairs or drydock periods. • Reviewing the ship’s safety management system (SMS) and planned maintenance system (PMS) to ensure that pilot transfer procedures, training and maintenance are appropriately addressed. • Engaging with the ship’s classification society and flag Administration early, particularly where modifications may require approval. Safe pilot transfer also depends on how the operation is carried out in practice. Risks should be properly assessed and controlled for each transfer, both during the transfer itself and when the arrangement is prepared, rigged and recovered. Clear communication between the vessel and pilot should ensure that the required arrangement, including the ladder position and height above the water, is understood before the transfer. Appropriate PPE, effective supervision, and proper training and familiarisation of those involved remain essential. Source: Gard, https://www.gard.no/en/insights/safe-pilot-transfer-operation/ 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Pilot transfer operation: A safer step aboard in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 26/10/2026 Safe pilot transfer operations depend on both correct procedures and fit-for-purpose equipment.

articles.body: China takes 81.8% of global new ship orders in first nine months, cementing its lead in shipbuilding market in Shipbuilding News 26/10/2026 Statistics on China’s shipbuilding industry for the January‑September period, released by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) on Friday, show that China continues to lead the world in the three key shipbuilding indicators. According to MIIT, in the first nine months of 2026, China completed 58.05 million deadweight tonnes (DWT) of shipbuilding output, a year‑on‑year rise of 50.7 percent. China’s shipbuilding output, new orders and order backlog accounted for 63.6 percent, 81.8 percent and 72.4 percent of the respective global market shares, MIIT data shows. Beyond the robust performance of the three core indicators, China is accelerating the green transition of its shipbuilding sector. It secured 74.1 percent of the global new-order market for green-powered vessels, up 5.7 percentage points from the January-June period. articles.body: HD Hyundai, Kiewit join forces to build advanced U.S. shipyard by 2029 in Shipbuilding News 26/10/2026 HD Hyundai is joining forces with U.S. construction giant Kiewit to build a state-of-the-art shipyard in the United States by 2029. The joint venture aims to combine Korean shipbuilding expertise with American industrial construction capabilities as the two countries seek to strengthen shipbuilding cooperation. The two companies formed a strategic partnership in July and have since discussed joint shipbuilding projects in the United States. Several potential sites in the southern and western United States are under consideration, with construction targeted to begin in 2027 and operations scheduled to start in 2029. The shipyard is also projected to employ around 3,000 people once it becomes fully operational. Although the investment amount and ownership structure have yet to be finalized, HD Hyundai is considering taking a majority stake. The new facility will be the first shipyard in the United States to adopt HD Hyundai’s Future of Shipyard model, which the company is developing in Korea. At the heart of the model is digital twin technology, which creates a virtual replica of a physical shipyard to monitor material locations, production progress and work being carried out on individual vessels across different sections of the facility in real time. Automated production systems and robotic welding will also be introduced to help address the shortage of skilled workers in the United States. The new joint shipbuilder will pursue contracts to build logistics support vessels for the U.S. Navy and commercial ships. The joint venture will also consider supplying shipbuilding blocks and modules to other U.S. shipyards and expanding into infrastructure projects, including port cranes used to load and unload shipping containers. Shipbuilding blocks are large prefabricated sections of a vessel’s hull, while modules are preassembled units containing piping, machinery and electrical equipment. By sourcing these components, U.S. shipyards can reduce the amount of fabrication and assembly work required on-site. “The launch of the joint venture marks an important milestone that demonstrates HD Hyundai’s commitment and vision as a strategic partner of the U.S. shipbuilding industry,” said Choi Han-nae, head of corporate planning at HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering. “We will contribute to rebuilding the U.S. shipbuilding industry, expanding shipbuilding cooperation between Korea and the United States and continuously pursue finding new opportunities.” Source: Korea JoongAng Daily 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: China’s Zhoushan overtakes Fujairah to become third-largest global bunker port in Port News 26/10/2026 China’s Zhoushan overtook Fujairah to become the world’s third-largest bunkering port in 2025, highlighting the growing prominence of Chinese ports in the global marine fuel market, according to rankings released at the ninth International Petroleum and Natural Gas Enterprises Conference in Zhoushan, Zhejiang province. Zhoushan supplied 8.54 million mt of marine fuel in 2025, placing it behind Singapore and Rotterdam but ahead of Antwerp-Bruges and Fujairah, according to the rankings. Singapore maintained its position as the world’s largest bunkering hub, with sales rising 3.8% year over year to 56.18 million mt. Rotterdam ranked second with 9.36 million mt. Antwerp-Bruges ranked fourth at 7.62 million mt, while Fujairah slipped behind Zhoushan to fifth place with 7.27 million mt. Zhoushan had ranked fourth globally in the previous ranking, closely trailing third-placed Fujairah, making its move into third place a notable shift in competition among the world’s major bunker hubs. Zhoushan strengthens bunker position Zhoushan’s bonded bunker fuel sales rose 10.1% year over year in 2025 on a comparable basis, according to data presented at the conference, extending growth at one of China’s key international bunkering centers. The port also supplied 515,500 mt of marine fuel to the domestic market during the year. The world’s 10 largest bunkering ports supplied a combined 116.7 million mt of marine fuels in 2025, up 3.3% year over year, indicating resilient bunker demand despite uncertainties surrounding international trade and financial policies. Zhoushan was among several Asian ports to record higher bunker sales during the year, alongside Hong Kong, Busan and Shanghai. The rankings highlighted the growing importance of Asian bunkering markets as shifts in global trade flows and shipping routes reshape competition among major fueling hubs. Chinese suppliers maintain strong presence Chinese companies also featured prominently among the world’s largest marine fuel suppliers in 2025. Chimbusco ranked first with sales of 28.16 million mt, broadly unchanged from 28.2 million mt in the previous year, according to the conference data. Sinopec Fuel Oil Sales Co. ranked third, with 2025 sales of 21.27 million mt, down 10.6% from 23.8 million mt a year earlier, according to the data. The top 10 global marine fuel suppliers recorded combined sales of 167 million mt in 2025, down 1.91% from 2024. The supplier ranking was based on marine fuel volumes sold directly to end-users, including contracted volumes and deliveries completed through third parties, while excluding inter-company trading volumes. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed the Zhoushan-delivered 380 CST fuel oil at $843/mt on Oct. 21. The premium over benchmark FOB Singapore 380 CST fuel oil cargoes rose $4.43/mt day over day to $77.82/mt. Platts assessed the Zhoushan-delivered LSFO at $925/mt on Oct. 21, down $20/mt day over day. The premium over the benchmark FOB Singapore 0.5%S marine fuel fell $5.32/mt to $70.50/mt. Source: Platts 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Singapore Conducts World’s Largest Ethanol Bunkering Operation in Port News 26/10/2026 Maersk, Golden Island Pte Ltd. and PSA Singapore (PSA) successfully completed Singapore’s first ethanol bunkering operation at PSA’s Pasir Panjang Terminal today, with the support of the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA). The operation was conducted simultaneously with cargo operations (SIMOPS), with bioethanol bunkered using a mass flow meter (MFM). Maersk Halifax, a Singapore-registered dual-fuel container vessel, was bunkered with approximately 5000 metric tonnes of ISCC-certified bioethanol from Golden Island’s Singapore-registered IMO Type II chemical tanker, M.T. Golden Centaurus, while container operations were carried out concurrently. This was the largest volume of ethanol bunkered in a single operation globally to date. The operation will provide data and learning points to assess how Singapore’s existing methanol bunkering technical reference, TR 129, could be adapted for ethanol bunkering. Ethanol has similar handling characteristics to methanol and can be used in methanol-capable engines, subject to the necessary modifications. The findings will also inform whether existing MFM systems can be used for future ethanol bunkering operations. Safety-First Approach Prior to the SIMOPS, participating parties conducted a Hazard Identification and Hazard and Operability Study workshop. MPA also worked closely with all stakeholders to ensure crew members were trained in handling the marine fuel and associated emergency responses, drawing on experience from methanol bunkering. Mr Ang Wee Keong, Chief Executive, MPA, said, “This operation allows us to test how Singapore’s experience and existing infrastructure for methanol bunkering can support another emerging marine fuel. The findings will help us develop the standards and procedures needed for safe and efficient ethanol bunkering, as we continue to prepare Singapore for a multi-fuel future.” “The energy transition requires us to explore and scale solutions that can deliver real-world impact,” said Emma Mazhari, Head of Energy Markets, Maersk. “At Maersk, we continue to pursue a multi-fuel strategy because we recognise that no single fuel pathway can decarbonise global shipping on its own.” Mr Johnny Tan, Managing Director, Golden Island Pte Ltd, said, “We are proud to have delivered Singapore’s first ethanol bunkering, and to have done it alongside live cargo operations, using a mass flow meter. Our crew and Golden Centaurus built on what we learned in methanol bunkering and followed the same safety-first discipline. That let us deliver the largest single ethanol bunker to date safely and on time. We thank MPA, Maersk and PSA for their close collaboration. Golden Island will keep investing in the people, vessels and know-how needed to supply lower-carbon fuels, so that customers can choose the fuel that best meets their decarbonisation goals in the Port of Singapore.” Mr Nelson Quek, Regional CEO Southeast Asia, PSA International, said, “The successful completion of the SIMOPS at Pasir Panjang Terminal marks an important step in advancing our operational readiness for a wider range of lower-carbon fuel options, supporting PSA’s commitment to sustainability and the maritime industry’s decarbonisation efforts. Safety remains our foremost priority, and this operation provides valuable insights into how ethanol bunkering can be safely integrated with container terminal operations. PSA Singapore will continue to work closely with our partners to strengthen our capabilities, build operational resilience, and support the safe, efficient, and scalable adoption of new marine fuels as we enable a more sustainable maritime ecosystem.” Source: Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore 2026-10-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Spanish railway infrastructure manager Adif has awarded the operating contract for the Vitoria-Júndiz intermodal rail terminal to a consortium comprising MEDLOG Spain Logistic, part of the MSC Group, the port authorities of Bilbao and Pasaia, and regional institutions in Álava. The contract has an initial duration of six years, with the possibility of extensions up to a maximum of 20 years. The TERMINAL INTERMODAL JÚNDIZ joint venture plans to handle approximately 300,000 intermodal transport units (ITUs) during the initial six-year period. The award is expected to strengthen rail freight connectivity between the Basque Country’s ports and inland logistics networks, supporting the development of the Atlantic Corridor and improving access to European markets. MEDLOG takes leading stake in terminal consortium MEDLOG holds the largest stake in the consortium at 40%, followed by the Bilbao Port Authority with 25%. The Vitoria-Gasteiz Intermodal Transport Centre (CTV) and the Álava Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Services each hold 15%, while the Pasaia Port Authority and Servicios Intermodales Bilbaoport (Sibport) each control 2.5%. The consortium expects annual throughput to increase progressively during the initial operating period, starting with 15,000 ITUs in the first year and 45,000 in the second year. Volumes are projected to reach 60,000 ITUs annually during each of the following four years, compared with the 4,723 ITUs handled at the terminal in 2025. These figures represent the consortium’s projected traffic volumes rather than confirmed future throughput. The terminal occupies approximately 55,000 square metres, including a 36,000-square-metre concrete handling area and three dead-end railway tracks with electrified sections at their termini. Additional facilities include internal roads, an administration and services building, and dedicated parking areas for heavy and light vehicles. Strengthening the Port of Bilbao’s hinterland connections The Júndiz logistics hub forms part of the Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T) and occupies a strategic position along the Atlantic Corridor. It is also located at the starting point of the Vitoria–San Sebastián–Bayonne–Bordeaux cross-border section, connecting freight transport networks across northern Spain and southwestern France. For the Port of Bilbao, the operating contract represents an opportunity to expand its inland logistics reach and strengthen rail-based freight connections. “The final award of the Júndiz rail terminal contract is wonderful news for Álava, the Basque Country and the Port of Bilbao,” said Ivan Jimenez Aira, President of the Bilbao Port Authority. “It represents recognition of a solid and ambitious project, the result of collaboration between public institutions and private companies that share the same strategic vision,” he added. Jimenez also highlighted the importance of improving rail connectivity and developing more competitive logistics services for companies operating in the region. The participation of MEDLOG alongside the two port authorities brings together shipping-related logistics operations and public infrastructure stakeholders within a single terminal management structure. The consortium aims to increase rail freight activity, improve regional logistics competitiveness and reinforce Álava’s position as an inland freight hub serving the Atlantic Corridor.

articles.body: Europe Gas Panagiotidis moves another LPG carrier in $18m fleet reshuffle Adis Ajdin October 26, 2026 0 94 1 minute read Roland Delhaxhe / Marine Traffic Roland Delhaxhe / Marine Traffic Greek shipowner Petros Panagiotidis is continuing to rearrange his LPG fleet across Nasdaq-listed companies, with AI OKTO agreeing to sell the 2015-built Dream Arrax to sister company Robin Energy for $18m. The latest transaction involves the 5,000 cu m gas carrier moving between two companies controlled by Panagiotidis, who serves as chairman and chief executive of both businesses. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary conditions. Robin Energy intends to finance the purchase using existing cash resources. Once completed, the acquisition will lift Robin’s fleet to three LPG carriers, while AI OKTO will be left with a single 5,000 cu m gas carrier. The move represents another transfer of existing tonnage within the Panagiotidis-controlled group rather than an expansion of the group’s combined fleet. The transaction follows the reorganisation unveiled in September, when Toro Corp moved to separate its remaining two LPG carriers, Dream Arrax and Dream Vermax , into AI OKTO. The earlier restructuring was itself part of a longer series of vessel transfers and corporate spin-offs involving Toro, Castor Maritime and Robin Energy. The four LPG carriers originally entered the group in 2023, when Toro acquired a quartet of Japanese-built 5,000 cu m ships for $70.7m. Two vessels subsequently moved to Robin through separate related-party sales: Dream Syrax for $18m and Dream Terrax for $20m. With the latest agreement, Dream Arrax is now set to follow them, leaving Dream Vermax as AI OKTO’s sole ship. Earlier coverage identified Dream Arrax as operating on a six-month charter at $371,500 per month, running to approximately November or December, with an extension option subject to agreement. (Source: Ansgar Walk) By Thomas Seal Oct 26, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Dubai’s DP World Ltd. is set to unveil a deal backing potential development of Canada’s port of Churchill, a northern outpost that Prime Minister Mark Carney aims to expand for exports to Europe and other markets. The global port operator has negotiated a memorandum of understanding with two Canadian entities, including Arctic Gateway Group, the owner and operator of the Churchill port and an associated railway, according to two people familiar with the matter who requested they not be identified. The agreement focuses on port operations and a possible transportation corridor to link Churchill with DP World’s global logistics network and inland port facilities managed by CentrePort Canada Inc. Churchill is a remote town in the north of the Canadian province of Manitoba. It sits on Hudson Bay, which connects to the Atlantic Ocean via Arctic waterways. Its location means that it could someday become a gateway to ship Canadian resources like liquefied natural gas, grain, potash and other critical minerals to customers in the Middle East and Europe. But doing all of that would take tens of billions of dollars of investment. Canada and the United Arab Emirates have been developing closer economic ties since Carney came to office last year with an agenda to build his country’s trade and investment connections with the rest of the world after US President Donald Trump started a trade war. Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan, the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, is scheduled to visit Ottawa on Monday and Tuesday, Carney’s office announced on Sunday. Last year, the UAE committed to invest C$70 billion ($49.9 billion) in Canada. “At a time of profound global transformation, Canada and the UAE are working to deepen their partnership and build greater economic strength, shared security, and long-term prosperity for people in both countries,” Carney’s office said . Canadian Energy Minister Tim Hodgson told Bloomberg News last year that Churchill has “tremendous potential” as a much larger export hub. The bay is currently frozen for most of the year, but Hodgson said it could be opened up for extended shipping seasons with icebreakers. Canada signed a deal for new ice-breaking ships in August. Read More: Canada Eyes Arctic Ocean Port to Ship Gas, Commodities to Europe Discussions about the port advanced during September meetings between UAE officials and Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew at the time of the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto in mid-September. A prospectus shared by Canada’s government with summit attendees put the price tag of a major expansion of Churchill and supporting infrastructure at $57 billion, with “preliminary investment requests” of $3.9 billion. That pitchbook said the initiative is to turn Churchill “into a four-season trade gateway through an LNG export corridor, rail upgrades, port modernization, and develop all-weather road access.” DP World already has extensive interests in Canada. It currently operates the container port in Prince Rupert on Canada’s west coast, and last year won the contract to operate a new terminal near Montreal. articles.title: Seatrium Inks $390M Deal to Complete Four Offshore Rigs for Keppel’s Rigco
articles.summary: Singapore's Seatrium has secured an agreement with Keppel's subsidiary RigCo to complete construction work on four offshore drilling rigs under an existing master services arrangement, with the total estimated contract value exceeding $390 million…
articles.body: Seatrium Inks $390M Deal to Complete Four Offshore Rigs for Keppel’s Rigco Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 26, 2026 (Credit Seatrium) Singapore's Seatrium has secured an agreement with Keppel's subsidiary RigCo to complete construction work on four offshore drilling rigs under an existing master services arrangement, with the total estimated contract value exceeding $390 million (S$500 million). The four rigs comprise a premium seventh-generation drillship, a harsh environment jack-up and two mid-water semisubmersibles designed for operations in the harsh conditions of Northwest Europe. The construction work will be funded by existing cash retained in RigCo, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Keppel. The drillship is expected to be delivered to RigCo in 2027, followed by the harsh environment jack-up in 2028, positioning both units for charter opportunities and monetisation through the Keppel Offshore Fund. Construction plans for the remaining two semisubmersibles are still being assessed. The agreement comes as offshore drilling rig market conditions improve following more than a decade of limited newbuild activity and the progressive retirement of older units. Higher utilization rates, an ageing global drilling fleet and structural supply constraints are supporting the outlook for offshore rig demand, according to the companies. "The demand for deepwater and harsh environment rigs is expected to increase over the next several years, providing conducive conditions for new, long-term charters of premium rigs. RigCo has been working closely with customers on their requirements amid the tightening market for advanced offshore rigs," said Cindy Lim, Chief Executive Officer, Infrastructure of Keppel and Non-Executive Director of RigCo. The resumption of construction forms part of Keppel's programme, announced in July 2026, to progressively monetise up to 10 legacy offshore rigs through the Keppel Offshore Fund, managed by Keppel and co-invested with Apollo as a limited partner. RigCo currently owns six modern jack-up rigs that have been delivered and leased to customers since 2022, alongside the four uncompleted drilling units covered by the latest agreement.

The two companies extended the arrangement by three years in April 2025, with an option for a further three years. The framework covers engineering, procurement, fabrication, transportation, installation and pre-commissioning of offshore facilities in Saudi waters. NMDC Energy has also expanded its Saudi manufacturing presence through its 400,000 sq m fabrication yard at Ras Al Khair, which began production last year and has an annual capacity of 40,000 tonnes. articles.body: Collaboration October 26, 2026 · 1 hour ago Minesto enters MoU in Maldives for tidal energy development NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Minesto Swedish ocean energy developer Minesto has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Morteza Capital, a Maldives- and Indian Ocean-focused investment and development firm, to develop commercial tidal energy opportunities in the Maldives. The partners will jointly pursue commercial project opportunities in the Maldives. The collaboration combines Minesto's technology and technical expertise with Morteza Capital's regional market knowledge, established stakeholder networks and capabilities in project development and investment structuring. "The transition away from diesel-based electricity generation is challenging for island communities, particularly where preserving the natural environment is essential to the local economy. The Maldives is a market where our technology has the potential to make a real difference," said Martin Edlund , CEO of Minesto. "Our collaboration with Morteza aligns perfectly with our go-to-market strategy. We seek to combine our technology and tidal energy know-how with strong local expertise and commercial development capabilities to pursue tidal deployment opportunities." Minesto has secured funding from the Nordic Project Fund (Nopef) to support market development activities in the Maldives, which it plans to use to support continued development of opportunities in the market. The MoU with Morteza Capital forms part of the Swedish company's broader strategy to accelerate international market development through close long-term partnerships with local and regional energy project developers and investors. "The Maldives has ambitious but challenging renewable energy aspirations to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels. We see strong potential for Minesto's innovative tidal energy technology to help overcome these challenges. By combining Minesto's proven technology with our local networks, investment expertise and project development capabilities, we aim to create a pathway towards commercially viable tidal energy projects that support the country's energy transition while preserving its exceptional natural environment," said Ghaly Murthala , Managing Director of Morteza Capital. articles.body: Business Developments & Projects October 26, 2026 · 2 hours ago Samsung Heavy Industries unveils Canada-tailored FLNG solution SHI is streamlining LNG development with a standardized FLNG platform, while strengthening local partnerships across Canada's energy sector. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email FLNG Megugu's hull launch at SHI as South Korean shipyard continues to progress the unit's construction for Cedar LNG Source: Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI) With global demand for cleaner energy on the rise, South Korea’s Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI) is embedding itself into Canada’s energy ecosystem by showcasing a streamlined, standardized floating liquefied natural gas (FLNG) design, aiming to trim development timelines, slash project costs, and forge local partnerships across British Columbia to create new business opportunities. Samsung Heavy Industries has presented a standardized FLNG platform optimized for Canada’s natural gas market, providing a tailored solution for future LNG development. The company hosted the Canada FLNG Technical Forum in Vancouver on October 23, in cooperation with Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA) Vancouver, bringing together approximately 100 representatives from local resource developers, First Nations communities, government and financial institutions to discuss cooperation in the LNG segment. Wang-Keun Lee , Executive Vice President and Head of SHI’s Shipbuilding & Offshore Business Division, commented: “FLNG is a competitive solution that can connect Canada’s abundant natural gas resources with global markets. With our proven technology and tailored solutions, we aim to become a key partner supporting the growth of Canada’s LNG industry.” SHI, which emphasizes that Canada has abundant natural gas resources and favorable access to Asian markets, used the forum to highlight its standardized FLNG platform optimized for the country’s natural gas development and export environment. The company points out that FLNG, which enables natural gas produced onshore to be liquefied and stored at sea before being exported, is drawing growing attention as an environmentally friendly and economically viable alternative for LNG development. With seven of the 11 newbuild FLNG orders placed worldwide already secured, Samsung Heavy Industries is building on the engineering expertise accumulated through these projects through a standardized FLNG platform for the Canadian market. “The standardized platform reduces repetitive new-design work and allows SHI to focus on meeting and optimizing project-specific requirements, helping optimize overall project timelines and improve investment efficiency,” underlined the South Korean player. The firm introduced Cedar FLNG as a representative project tailored to the Canadian market. The work on this floating facility, which weighs approximately 50,000 tonnes, was awarded to SHI in 2024 and launched in June. The unit will be deployed off Kitimat, British Columbia, where it will receive natural gas through an onshore pipeline, liquefy and store the gas offshore, and transfer the LNG to carriers for export. The FLNG is expected to play an important role in supporting Canada’s LNG exports. SHI further explained that the forum in Vancouver featured a range of discussions aimed at connecting its standardized FLNG platform with actual projects, as LNG developers shared their experience in advancing projects, while participating financial institutions presented approaches to financing support. Given that government permitting, gas supply and infrastructure, and the participation of First Nations require cooperation among multiple stakeholders in Canada, the South Korean firm explored concrete areas of collaboration with government representatives, LNG developers, First Nations communities, and financial institutions across the broader LNG ecosystem. Samsung Heavy Industries plans to move beyond the role of an EPC contractor by providing tailored solutions from the early stages of project development and working closely with local partners, with the aim of supporting future LNG projects in Canada while creating new opportunities in the global FLNG market. Stuart Taylor , Cedar LNG’s Executive Advisor, underscored: “SHI’s floating LNG solution could bring significant benefits to Canada’s LNG industry by helping optimize project cost and overall development schedule while minimizing environmental impact and preserving Canada’s natural environment.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! October 26, 2026 Prospector 5 jack-up rig (Credit: Screenshot/Youtube) Borr Drilling's Prospector 5 jack-up rig has sunk offshore Gabon after experiencing a punch-through event during preload operations that caused it to lose stability, leaving five people missing and 110 safely accounted for among the 115 personnel on board. In its latest update on October 26, Borr Drilling said extensive marine and air search and rescue operations were continuing for the five missing individuals, while the 110 personnel accounted for were being brought ashore in Gabon, where care and support was being provided. Reuters reported on October 25, citing three sources familiar with the matter, that one Indian national had been found dead, leaving four people missing, including three Gabonese nationals and another expatriate. However, the Gabonese government had not confirmed the reported death, maintaining that five people remained missing. Borr Drilling's latest update also continued to list five individuals as unaccounted for, without confirming any fatalities. The incident occurred at approximately 20:37 local time on October 24 while the Prospector 5 was conducting jacking operations in preparation for a planned drilling campaign on BW Energy's Dussafu Marine licence offshore Gabon. The rig, owned and operated by Borr Drilling, was contracted to support BW Energy's offshore drilling operations. Borr Drilling said its onshore emergency response team was working with local authorities and BW Energy to respond to the incident, support those affected and continue the search for missing personnel. The company is also in contact with the families of the missing personnel. "We are deeply concerned for those who remain unaccounted for and everyone affected by this incident. Our immediate priority is supporting the ongoing search and rescue efforts and the welfare of all personnel involved," said Bruno Morand, Borr Drilling CEO, in the company's initial statement on October 25. MaBoMo Production Shut Down Following Rig Incident BW Energy confirmed that production at its MaBoMo facility on the Dussafu licence had been shut down in accordance with standard procedures during ongoing drilling preparations. The company said there had been no reported damage to the facility or related equipment, nor any accidental discharge of harmful substances into the sea from the facility. BW Energy added it was supporting the ongoing search and rescue operations in close coordination with Borr Drilling, relevant authorities and emergency responders. Borr Drilling confirmed it was working with its partners and authorities to ensure a robust investigation into the cause of the incident, while emphasizing that its immediate priority remained the search for missing personnel and support for those affected. Built in 2014, the Prospector 5 is an F&G JU-2000E type jack-up drilling rig with a maximum operating water depth of 400 feet and a maximum drilling depth of 35,000 feet.

articles.title: ClassNK releases new framework for onboard carbon capture systems
articles.summary: Japanese classification society ClassNK has released a new handbook providing guidance on the implementation of onboard carbon capture systems (OCCS), addressing the technical, regulatory and infrastructure requirements involved in capturing and managing carbon dioxide emissions from ships. Published on October 23,...
articles.body: Japanese classification society ClassNK has released a new handbook providing guidance on the implementation of onboard carbon capture systems (OCCS), addressing the technical, regulatory and infrastructure requirements involved in capturing and managing carbon dioxide emissions from ships. Published on October 23, 2026, the handbook, titled Onboard Carbon Capture Systems Implementation Framework , forms part of ClassNK’s Handbook on Ship GHG Emissions Evaluation series. The publication is intended to support shipowners, operators and other maritime stakeholders considering the introduction of onboard carbon capture technology, providing a framework for assessing projects across the entire CO₂ management value chain. According to ClassNK, successful implementation requires more than the installation of capture equipment aboard vessels. It also depends on the availability of infrastructure for unloading, transporting, storing or utilising captured CO₂, alongside reliable mechanisms for measuring and verifying emissions reductions. Addressing the full carbon capture value chain Onboard carbon capture systems are designed to capture CO₂ from ship exhaust gases, process it and temporarily store it aboard vessels before transferring it for further handling. While the technology is being explored as a potential option for reducing greenhouse gas emissions from shipping, its implementation involves technical and operational considerations extending beyond the vessel itself. The new handbook brings together requirements relating to onboard capture and storage, shoreside infrastructure, regulatory considerations and emissions-reduction assessment. Particular attention is given to Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) frameworks, which support the measurement and verification of emissions and emission reductions. The publication also addresses Chain of Custody (CoC) systems, which enable the tracking and management of captured CO₂ and its associated information throughout the supply chain. These mechanisms are relevant to determining how captured carbon is handled after leaving a vessel and how the resulting emissions reductions can be quantified and verified. Supporting maritime decarbonisation projects The publication builds on ClassNK’s previous work on onboard carbon capture technology, including its Guidelines for Onboard CO₂ Capture and Storage Systems . Through those guidelines, the classification society has developed safety and technical requirements for onboard capture and storage arrangements while accumulating knowledge from demonstration projects and greenhouse gas certification activities. The new handbook takes a broader approach by bringing together the considerations involved in planning and evaluating an entire OCCS project. ClassNK said the document is intended to facilitate discussions among relevant stakeholders and support the assessment of specific carbon capture initiatives. The guidance comes as the maritime industry continues to explore different approaches to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, including energy-efficiency improvements, alternative fuels and technologies capable of capturing emissions directly from vessel exhaust systems. ClassNK stated that it will continue supporting maritime decarbonisation efforts through the provision of technical information and guidance. The Onboard Carbon Capture Systems Implementation Framework is available through the classification society’s Transition Support Services website and its MyPage technical publications platform.

articles.title: VLCC delivery wave set to reach levels not seen since the 1970s
articles.summary: The VLCC sector is heading for its biggest delivery wave in half a century, with more than 100 new supertankers scheduled to enter service annually in both 2028 and 2029, according to Hartland Shipping Services. The scale recalls the supertanker boom of the 1970s. BIMCO’s historical figures put the all-time record at...
articles.body: Tankers VLCC delivery wave set to reach levels not seen since the 1970s Sam Chambers October 26, 2026 0 1,029 2 minutes read Hengli Group Hengli Group The VLCC sector is heading for its biggest delivery wave in half a century, with more than 100 new supertankers scheduled to enter service annually in both 2028 and 2029, according to Hartland Shipping Services. The scale recalls the supertanker boom of the 1970s. BIMCO’s historical figures put the all-time record at 116 VLCCs delivered in 1974. Since then, even the 68 deliveries recorded in 2019 represented a four-decade high. The historical precedent is worth noting. A wave of tankers ordered during the early 1970s boom arrived just as the 1973 oil shock devastated demand. Between 1974 and 1975, global oil trade plunged 23% while tanker capacity grew nearly 16%, according to UNCTAD. Freight rates collapsed. The reopening of the Suez Canal in 1975 further shortened voyages. By year-end, 573 tankers representing 47.8m dwt were laid up, according to INTERTANKO. Owners faced financial ruin, newbuildings went straight into lay-up and the industry endured a prolonged depression. Hartland now counts 319 VLCCs on order, equivalent to 34% of the existing fleet, rising to 42% when sanctioned ships are excluded. Yet just 20 are scheduled for delivery over the next six months. Only six VLCCs delivered last year and just one in 2024. This could be an upcoming supply disaster Of the current orderbook, 138 ships are not due until 2029 or later. BRS paints a similarly picture, allocating 283 of its 351 VLCC orders to 2028 onwards. Whether this unprecedented modern influx destroys earnings or simply replaces an ageing fleet is debatable. Hartland notes that 47% of VLCCs are already at least 15 years old. Investment bank Jefferies is among the optimists, arguing last week that “we see most newbuilds as replacements”. It expects tanker rates to ease more slowly than the market anticipates, potentially extending the cycle beyond 2029. The difficulty with this argument is that owners are showing little appetite for scrapping. Banchero Costa records just four VLCC demolitions during the first nine months of 2026, despite 172 new orders over the same period. Clarksons currently values a 15-year-old VLCC at $165m, considerably more than the $131.5m required to order a newbuilding. Extraordinary earnings and secondhand prices are keeping ageing tonnage trading. Banchero Costa projects net VLCC fleet growth of 4% this year and 5.7% in 2027, compared with just 0.2% in 2025. Meanwhile, seaborne crude loadings fell 6% year-on-year during January-September. Demand could become an equally serious problem. Braemar warns that today’s exceptionally expensive freight is already encouraging Asian refiners to favour shorter-haul Middle Eastern crude over Atlantic barrels, eroding tonne-mile demand. It also identifies a growing surplus of VLCCs in the Middle East as ship-to-ship activity slows. For now, geopolitical disruption and limited vessel availability are sustaining extraordinary earnings. The danger is that today’s supply shortage is encouraging the ordering spree that could eventually bring the boom crashing down. “This could be an upcoming supply disaster or merely some much needed fleet replacement,” Hartland stated in its latest weekly report.
