articles.title: Black Sea bloodshed outstrips Hormuz
articles.summary: A relentless series of attacks on merchant ships and port infrastructure over the past four days has underscored the Black Sea’s emergence as the world’s deadliest shipping route, with seafarer fatalities this year now exceeding those recorded around the Strait of Hormuz. More than 570 vessels have been attacked in...
articles.body: Europe Operations Tankers Black Sea bloodshed outstrips Hormuz Sam Chambers October 26, 2026 0 586 2 minutes read X.com X.com A relentless series of attacks on merchant ships and port infrastructure over the past four days has underscored the Black Sea’s emergence as the world’s deadliest shipping route, with seafarer fatalities this year now exceeding those recorded around the Strait of Hormuz. More than 570 vessels have been attacked in the Black Sea during 2026, with at least 40 seafarers killed, according to figures compiled by maritime security firm Ambrey and the International Maritime Organization and reported by the Financial Times. By comparison, the IMO has confirmed 120 attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East, resulting in 24 seafarer deaths as of October 22. The latest Black Sea violence began on Friday when the Comoros-flagged Khoryv was struck by a drone approximately 13 nautical miles off Romania’s Constanta port. The 43-year-old vessel, sailing from Türkiye towards the Danube port of Sulina, capsized following the strike. One seafarer was killed, three remain missing and nine were rescued. Romanian president Nicușor Dan blamed Russia for the attack, describing it as another escalation of Moscow’s war against Ukraine. A Romanian navigational warning issued on Sunday confirms the vessel remains partially submerged and capsized, drifting south of its original position. Ships have been instructed to maintain a distance of at least one nautical mile. Friday also saw Russia claim strikes against port facilities at Vylkove on the Danube, including installations allegedly used for operating unmanned surface vessels. Moscow separately claimed to have struck a cargo ship heading for Odesa. On Saturday, Russia’s defence ministry reported further attacks against Chornomorsk, claiming to have destroyed a workshop manufacturing unmanned surface vessels. It also claimed another strike against a cargo ship bound for Odesa. The attacks reportedly continued on Sunday, with Moscow claiming two more cargo vessel strikes, one against a ship heading for Chornomorsk overnight and another bound for Odesa during the day. Today, Russia announced another attack against a cargo ship heading for Odesa, alongside strikes on cargo-handling infrastructure at three berthing terminals in Chornomorsk. The Russian claims concerning these additional vessels and port installations have not been independently verified. The identities of the ships remain unknown, and it is unclear whether successive announcements involve separate vessels. The escalation extends well beyond Ukrainian territorial waters. Ambrey records nine merchant vessels struck in Romanian and Bulgarian waters during October, including several ships sunk or badly damaged close to the coastlines of the two NATO members. The security consultancy has warned that merchant vessels cannot be assured of protection from drones operating near NATO territory. NATO has announced additional maritime patrol aircraft, surveillance equipment and drones to strengthen monitoring of the region. The commercial repercussions are becoming increasingly severe. War-risk insurance premiums for some Black Sea voyages have climbed to as much as 15% of a vessel’s hull value, roughly twice the levels reported for the Persian Gulf. The Joint War Committee has also expanded its listed area to cover almost the entire Black Sea, excluding the territorial waters of Türkiye, Romania, Bulgaria and Georgia. articles.title: Panama Canal reopens last-minute slots amid traffic recovery
articles.summary: The Panama Canal has restored last-minute transit reservations for ships using its panamax locks, easing one of the restrictions introduced during this year’s drought-related disruption. The canal authority confirmed that the service resumed on October 21, allowing operators to secure short-notice passage when slots...
articles.body: Americas Containers Dry Cargo Gas Tankers Panama Canal reopens last-minute slots amid traffic recovery Adis Ajdin October 26, 2026 0 681 1 minute read Panama Canal Authority Panama Canal Authority The Panama Canal has restored last-minute transit reservations for ships using its panamax locks, easing one of the restrictions introduced during this year’s drought-related disruption. The canal authority confirmed that the service resumed on October 21, allowing operators to secure short-notice passage when slots become available. The additional reservations will be offered at the authority’s discretion, depending on operational capacity and availability. The move follows improvements in rainfall and water-saving measures that have helped stabilise operations at the waterway. However, the authority warned that the watershed continues to face a water deficit and that ships without confirmed bookings could still experience substantial delays. The easing comes after the canal closed its 2026 financial year with record cargo tonnage. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits during the 12 months to September 30, up 4.1% year on year, while tonnage increased 6.5% to 521m Panama Canal measurement tons. Neopanamax traffic accounted for 52.2% of total tonnage, with volumes through the larger locks rising 8.2% compared with the previous financial year. The latest measures follow a series of adjustments to transit capacity as the canal responds to shifting trade patterns and fluctuating water levels. In September, the authority reduced daily booking capacity to 32 vessels before improving conditions allowed an additional Neopanamax slot to be restored from October 15, bringing the total to 33. The canal has also been expanding its longer-term reservation arrangements. Earlier this month, it introduced plans to extend its Long-term Slot Allocation programme to panamax vessels for the first time. That programme will cover January 3 to April 3, 2027, providing 288 Panamax slots alongside 270 neopanamax slots through competitive allocations in November. The latest advisory introduces another change affecting operators using the original locks. From January 3, 2027, booking swaps and substitutions between shipping alliance members will be extended to vessels in the panamax super category, arrangements previously available only to neopanamax ships. The authority said existing booking rules otherwise remain in place. articles.body: Business & Finance October 26, 2026 · 4 hours ago Seatrium rakes in millions with Keppel’s RigCo to revive four stranded rigs Keppel’s RigCo has enlisted Seatrium to finish construction of four premium offshore rigs in a deal worth over S$500 million ($391 million). MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Jack-up rig (for illustration purposes) Source: Keppel As aging global fleets and heightened energy security concerns drive renewed demand for offshore drilling, RigCo, a wholly owned subsidiary of Keppel, has partnered with Singapore’s Seatrium to complete the construction of four legacy offshore rigs. The initiative positions RigCo to capitalize on a tightening offshore drilling market while paving the way for potential asset monetization through the Keppel Offshore Fund. Under an existing master services arrangement, the duo will collaborate on the completion of construction work in respect of four offshore rigs owned by Keppel’s subsidiary, which comprise a premium seventh-generation drillship , a harsh environment jack-up , and two mid-water semi-submersibles suited to work in the harshest environments of Northwest Europe. Cindy Lim , Chief Executive Officer at Infrastructure of Keppel and Non-Executive Director of RigCo, commented: “The demand for deepwater and harsh environment rigs is expected to increase over the next several years, providing conducive conditions for new, long-term charters of premium rigs. RigCo has been working closely with customers on their requirements amid the tightening market for advanced offshore rigs. “The resumption of construction work marks an important milestone in Keppel's strategy to transform RigCo’s work-in-progress offshore rigs into high-quality, income-generating assets. Their phased completion is part of Keppel’s program, announced in July 2026, to progressively monetize up to 10 legacy rigs through the Keppel Offshore Fund, managed by Keppel, and co-invested with Apollo as limited partner.” Related Articles Fossil Energy Keppel taking back control over 13 rigs in hot pursuit of monetization during offshore drilling upcycle 4 min read The total estimated contract value for the construction of all four rigs of more than S$500 million will be funded by existing cash retained in RigCo, which has six modern jack-ups that have been delivered and leased to customers beginning in 2022. The company’s remaining uncompleted assets include a harsh environment jack-up, a premium drillship, and two harsh environment semi-submersibles. The drillship and the harsh environment jack-up are expected to be delivered to Keppel’s subsidiary in 2027 and 2028, respectively, positioning them for charters and supporting monetization through the Keppel Offshore Fund, while construction plans for the remaining two rigs are being assessed. Related Articles Business & Finance Keppel to divest six operational rigs through new private fund for $936 million 2 min read William Gu , Executive Vice President of Seatrium Energy (Marketing), said: “Seatrium has a long and distinguished global track record for the full lifecycle of high specification offshore rigs from design to build, upgrades, life extension and operational optimi\ation. Today, more than two-thirds of the world's operational jack-up rigs are based on Seatrium's designs, including one of the units for RigCo. “This award reflects our undisputed capabilities to deliver complex projects safely, efficiently and to the highest quality standards. We look forward to leveraging our integrated capabilities and execution excellence to support RigCo in realizing the full potential of these premium assets.” Alongside the heightened need for energy security, the resumption of rig construction is expected to create value for both companies. RigCo emphasizes that offshore rig market fundamentals are improving, underpinned by higher utilization rates, an aging global drilling fleet, and structural supply constraints, following more than a decade of limited newbuild activity and the progressive retirement of older rigs. articles.title: Readers Speak: Cyberattacks emerge as the leading threat to cargo security
articles.summary: Cargo security has become an increasingly complex concern for the shipping and logistics industry, with physical risks now accompanied by threats involving digital systems, identity fraud and internal access. In its latest Readers Speak poll, Container News asked readers: “What is the biggest threat to cargo...
articles.body: Cargo security has become an increasingly complex concern for the shipping and logistics industry, with physical risks now accompanied by threats involving digital systems, identity fraud and internal access. In its latest Readers Speak poll, Container News asked readers: “What is the biggest threat to cargo security?” The results identified cyberattacks as the leading concern, ahead of cargo theft, insider threats and identity fraud. While the responses reflect different perceptions of risk, they also highlight the range of vulnerabilities that shipping and logistics businesses must consider when protecting cargo throughout the supply chain. Cyberattacks lead cargo security concerns Cyberattacks emerged as the most frequently selected threat, indicating that digital security occupies a prominent position in readers’ assessments of cargo-related risks. Modern cargo movements depend on interconnected information systems supporting bookings, shipment documentation, tracking, terminal operations and cargo release procedures. Disruption or manipulation of these systems can create operational difficulties and potentially expose sensitive information. The poll’s findings suggest that readers recognise the importance of protecting the digital infrastructure supporting cargo movements, alongside the physical protection of shipments. However, the results reflect perceived threats rather than measured incident frequency or financial losses. They should not be interpreted as evidence that cyberattacks cause more cargo-related damage than other forms of criminal activity. Physical cargo theft remains a major concern Cargo theft also attracted substantial support, reinforcing its continuing relevance within the industry’s security priorities. Unlike cyberattacks, physical theft directly involves the unlawful removal of goods from trucks, warehouses, terminals or other points along the logistics chain. Its prominence in the poll suggests that traditional security challenges remain important even as digital vulnerabilities attract growing attention. The findings therefore point to a security environment in which physical protection and digital safeguards should not be treated as competing priorities. Insider threats and identity fraud highlight additional vulnerabilities Insider threats and identity fraud received less support than cyberattacks and physical theft, but both represent distinct areas of concern. Insider threats involve risks associated with individuals who possess legitimate access to facilities, systems or operational information. Such access can potentially be misused to facilitate unauthorised cargo movements or expose sensitive shipment details. Identity fraud, meanwhile, involves impersonation or the use of false credentials to obtain access to goods or logistics processes. Examples may include fraudulent carrier identities or manipulated collection instructions. Although these threats attracted fewer responses, their inclusion highlights the importance of access controls, identity verification and internal security procedures. It is also important to recognise that these categories can overlap. A cargo theft incident, for example, may involve fraudulent identification or assistance from someone with legitimate operational access. How this fits into the broader Readers Speak trend Previous Readers Speak polls have explored the industry’s concerns about geopolitical disruptions, shipping resilience, port infrastructure and operational uncertainty. The latest findings add cargo security to that wider discussion, shifting attention towards the vulnerabilities that can affect individual shipments and the systems supporting their movement. The prominence of cyberattacks suggests that readers view digital exposure as a central security concern. At the same time, the continued support for physical cargo theft and the recognition of insider threats and identity fraud indicate that cargo protection remains a multidimensional challenge. The overall message is that effective cargo security requires attention to both physical operations and the digital processes connecting the international supply chain.

articles.title: Wärtsilä and WinGD renew global marine engine service agreement
articles.summary: Wärtsilä and WinGD have signed a new long-term Service Framework Agreement to ensure continued technical support and maintenance services for two-stroke marine engines operating across the global shipping fleet. Announced on October 23, 2026, the agreement reinforces a service relationship established in 2015 and...
articles.body: Wärtsilä and WinGD have signed a new long-term Service Framework Agreement to ensure continued technical support and maintenance services for two-stroke marine engines operating across the global shipping fleet. Announced on October 23, 2026, the agreement reinforces a service relationship established in 2015 and confirms Wärtsilä’s continued position as an authorised global service provider for WinGD, Wärtsilä and Sulzer-branded two-stroke engines. Under the agreement, shipowners and operators will retain access to the service capabilities of both companies, including technical expertise, maintenance support and lifecycle services designed to support engine reliability and operational continuity. The arrangement also aims to help vessel operators plan maintenance activities and prepare their fleets for evolving marine technologies, alternative fuels and decarbonisation requirements. Maintaining global engine support capabilities The renewed agreement combines Wärtsilä’s international service network with WinGD’s own service offering, Global Service by WinGD, providing customers with continued access to authorised technical support across different generations of two-stroke engines. “Our promise to customers is trusted, responsive and reliable support throughout the complete lifecycle of their engines; anytime, anywhere,” said Dominik Schneiter, CEO of WinGD. Schneiter explained that the agreement complements WinGD’s existing service operations while ensuring uninterrupted support and access to expertise suited to different engine generations. Wärtsilä will continue providing genuine spare parts, field services, workshop capabilities, technical assistance and long-term lifecycle agreements for the relevant installed engine base. “This agreement confirms the continuity of a long-standing service relationship that has supported WinGD’s installed base for over a decade,” said Roger Holm, President of Wärtsilä Marine and Executive Vice President at Wärtsilä Corporation. Holm added that the arrangement maintains access to Wärtsilä’s global service network and technical expertise throughout the operating life of customers’ engines. Building on a decade-long partnership The relationship between the two companies dates back to 2015, when Wärtsilä sold its two-stroke engine business to China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), leading to the formation of WinGD. WinGD continues to operate as an original equipment manufacturer, technology developer and global service provider for two-stroke engines carrying the WinGD, Wärtsilä and Sulzer names. Meanwhile, Wärtsilä has maintained its role in supporting the installed engine base through its international service organisation and experience in marine engine maintenance. The new Service Framework Agreement formalises the continuation of this relationship, providing shipowners and operators with access to authorised support from both organisations. The companies did not disclose the financial terms or specific duration of the agreement.

Announced on October 23, 2026, the agreement covers the development, major conversion and integration of hydrogen-ready floating power plants designed to provide electricity to national grids. Under the contract, Seatrium will undertake equipment integration, mechanical completion and pre-commissioning activities for the five vessels. Engineering work is already underway, with the first vessel scheduled to arrive at Seatrium’s Tuas Boulevard Yard in Singapore in December 2027. The agreement represents Seatrium’s first major conversion and integration project involving Karpowership’s Whale Class Powerships. Whale Class vessels designed for large-scale power generation Karpowership’s Whale Class represents its highest-capacity generation of floating power plants, designed to deliver up to 600 MW of electricity through hydrogen-ready, multi-fuel power generation systems. The vessels incorporate onboard substations that enable direct connections to national electricity grids. According to Karpowership, its plug-and-play Powership design can allow electricity generation to begin in as little as 30 days, depending on deployment requirements. The new generation is designed to combine substantial power generation capacity with a compact operational footprint and arrangements supporting continuous fuel supply. “This significant milestone marks Seatrium’s first major conversion work and integration of Karpowership’s Whale Class Powerships,” said Alvin Gan, Executive Vice President, Repairs and Upgrades, Seatrium. “We are proud to support Karpowership’s drive to pioneer innovative floating power solutions and the next phase of its fleet development, bringing our capabilities in complex vessel integration and offshore engineering to the project,” he added. Gokhan Kocak, Chief Technical Operations Officer at Karpowership, highlighted the companies’ established relationship and Seatrium’s experience in complex vessel integration. “The next-generation Whale Class Powerships demonstrate our continued commitment to innovation, operational excellence and energy security,” said Kocak. Partnership builds on previous FSRU conversion projects The latest contract follows a Letter of Intent signed by Seatrium and Karpowership in August 2025, which outlined plans for three floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) conversions and the potential integration of up to six new-generation Powerships. The newly announced agreement confirms conversion and integration work for five Whale Class vessels, marking a further step in the companies’ cooperation. Their relationship dates back to 2018, with Seatrium having completed seven FSRU conversion projects for Karpowership. The company also secured its eighth and ninth FSRU conversion projects during 2026. The latest award expands Seatrium’s involvement in Karpowership’s fleet development programme, combining the Singapore group’s marine engineering and conversion capabilities with Karpowership’s floating electricity generation technology. Karpowership operates a fleet of 45 Powerships with total installed generating capacity exceeding 8,500 MW, according to the company’s information accompanying the announcement. The financial value of the five-vessel contract and the expected completion dates for the individual conversions were not disclosed.

articles.title: Konecranes reports strong port equipment deliveries despite order slowdown

According to its interim financial report published on October 23, the...
articles.body: Finnish lifting equipment manufacturer Konecranes reported a strong recovery in port equipment deliveries during the third quarter of 2026, although new orders in its Port Solutions business declined significantly compared with the previous year. According to its interim financial report published on October 23, the company’s Port Solutions division recorded net sales of €420 million during July–September, representing an increase of 28.3% in comparable currencies. However, order intake in the division declined by 36.7% in comparable currencies to €288 million, reflecting volatility in the timing of customer orders. Despite the decline in new orders, the division’s comparable EBITA margin improved to 12.0%, compared with 11.8% in the corresponding period of 2025, supported primarily by higher delivery volumes. Konecranes said customer activity remained strong across its port equipment product lines, while the timing of new orders was unfavourable during the quarter. Port equipment deliveries support quarterly performance The contrasting performance between orders and sales highlights the impact of project timing on the company’s port equipment business. While Port Solutions experienced a significant reduction in quarterly order intake, deliveries accelerated, contributing to stronger revenue and improved profitability. CEO Marko Tulokas said the company’s third-quarter performance benefited from solid delivery execution, particularly within Port Solutions. The company also indicated that its Port Solutions order book remained approximately at the same level as a year earlier, despite the decline in quarterly orders. At group level, Konecranes reported third-quarter net sales of €1.10 billion, up 11.4% year-on-year, while total order intake decreased by 12.0% to €1.01 billion. Comparable EBITA increased to €172.2 million from €164.9 million, although the corresponding margin declined to 15.6% from 16.7%. For the first nine months of 2026, the group’s order intake reached €3.32 billion, while its order book increased by 8.0% to €3.30 billion. Container handling outlook remains positive Looking ahead, Konecranes maintained a positive long-term assessment of container handling activity, despite ongoing uncertainty surrounding international trade and geopolitical developments. The company noted that container throughput remained at elevated levels, supporting the longer-term prospects for demand in port equipment and container handling. However, Konecranes acknowledged that geopolitical uncertainty and trade policy tensions continued to affect the operating environment. The company reiterated its full-year 2026 financial guidance, expecting net sales to remain approximately unchanged or increase compared with 2025. It also expects its comparable EBITA margin to remain approximately at the previous year’s level. The results come as Konecranes continues implementing its updated strategy, announced in September, focusing on profitable growth, technological development and expanding its presence across existing business areas. For port operators, the company’s latest results indicate continued equipment deliveries and an active customer pipeline, although the timing of new investment commitments remains uneven.

articles.title: CEVA Logistics and Zalando advance AI-powered warehouse robotics
articles.summary: CEVA Logistics and Zalando are collaborating with Sereact, NVIDIA and Nebius on an artificial intelligence training system designed to improve robotic handling of e-commerce returns and accelerate the development of automated warehouse operations. Announced on October 22, 2026, the initiative introduces a closed-loop...
articles.body: CEVA Logistics and Zalando are collaborating with Sereact, NVIDIA and Nebius on an artificial intelligence training system designed to improve robotic handling of e-commerce returns and accelerate the development of automated warehouse operations. Announced on October 22, 2026, the initiative introduces a closed-loop training process for Cortex, Sereact’s robotic AI system, combining real-world warehouse data with simulation, model training and performance evaluation. The initial deployment targets Zalando’s returns handling operations at selected CEVA Logistics fulfillment centers, where robotic systems must process products arriving in varying conditions, packaging formats and configurations. According to the companies, the new approach is designed to shorten robotic training and improvement cycles from weeks to days, allowing systems to adapt more quickly to changing product assortments and operational requirements. AI simulation accelerates robotic training The system combines Sereact’s Cortex vision-language-action model with NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab and Cosmos technologies, supported by Nebius’ Physical AI Workbench. During warehouse operations, Sereact’s robotic stations collect data from actual returns handling activities, including video recordings and robotic movement information. These datasets are transferred to Nebius’ cloud infrastructure, where NVIDIA Isaac Lab generates simulated variations of real-world handling scenarios. NVIDIA Cosmos then produces additional variations involving different garment conditions, packaging materials and lighting environments. The expanded datasets are used to further train Cortex on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, enabling the robotic system to encounter a wider range of potential handling situations before updated software is tested in operational environments. Each updated policy is evaluated against predefined performance criteria established by Sereact. Successful versions proceed to real-world testing, while those that fail trigger additional simulation and training focused on the identified weaknesses. The process is coordinated through an AI agent using NVIDIA’s Physical AI Data Factory skills and Nebius’ Workbench framework. Engineers establish training objectives and approve operations exceeding predefined computing cost limits. Targeting complex e-commerce returns operations Returns handling presents particular challenges for warehouse automation because products can arrive folded, crumpled, unpackaged or without their original labels. Robotic systems must identify, pick, inspect and sort these items while adapting to changing product ranges and seasonal demand. Within the partnership, Sereact provides its Cortex AI model and dual-arm robotic returns stations, while NVIDIA supplies simulation and training technologies. Nebius provides the cloud infrastructure and development environment through its European data centers. CEVA Logistics hosts the robotic stations within its fulfillment operations for Zalando, which supplies the returns-handling use case for evaluating the technology. The companies aim to create a continuous improvement process in which data collected during warehouse operations can be used to develop and test updated robotic capabilities more efficiently. Beyond the initial logistics application, the closed-loop training pipeline is available as a reference architecture through Nebius’ Physical AI Workbench. The framework includes NVIDIA’s Physical AI Data Factory skills and is accessible to robotics development teams using Nebius AI Cloud, with computing and storage resources charged according to usage. The collaboration highlights efforts to integrate physical AI, cloud computing and robotic automation into complex fulfillment operations, particularly processes that require systems to adapt to unpredictable product conditions.

Sri Lanka Navy/Handout via REUTERS By Uditha Jayasinghe COLOMBO, Oct 25 (Reuters) – Sri Lanka coordinated the rescue of 40 Iranian sailors from multiple commercial ships in international waters off the coast of the country and supported their return to Iran, a spokesman for the island nation’s foreign ministry said on Sunday. REUTERS/Yoruk Isik MOSCOW, Oct 23 (Reuters) – Latvia, a member of the European Union and NATO, has emerged as one of the top five countries used to ship Russian grain this marketing season despite strained political ties, as Moscow redirects exports from the Azov-Black Sea basin to Baltic ports. Some 431,700 metric tons of Russian grain were shipped via Latvia between July and October, consultancy ProZerno said. Read Also: Baltic Block Of Russian Grain May Open Black Sea, Latvia Says The Latvian foreign ministry said in a statement that Russian grain imports have been banned in Latvia since 2024 and that while there is no transit ban in place yet, the government is working on that as either an EU or a national measure. Iran remained the largest buyer of Russian grain during the period, importing 1.716 million tons, helped by strong purchases of barley and corn. Russia has been reshaping its grain export routes after shipments through the Azov-Black Sea basin, its main export corridor, largely stalled in mid-August. Deep-water Baltic ports have become the main outlet, particularly for wheat. According to railway carrier and grain analyst Rusagrotrans, the Baltic route accounted for 65% of Russian grain exports in September. Exports are being shipped through both Russian Baltic ports and ports in the Baltic states, chiefly Latvia. Estonia has banned the transit of Russian grain through its territory, while the Baltic states proposed earlier this month a European Union ban on Russian grain exports through the bloc. Shipments via the Caspian Sea have also risen sharply, with most cargoes destined for Iran. Oct 24 (Reuters) – Ras Al Khaimah authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice, a day after anoffshore oil leak prompted beach closures in neighboring Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah. The Public Services Department announced the closures in a statement shared by Ras Al Khaimah Police General Headquarters. No reason was given. The United Arab Emirates said on Friday that efforts were underway to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment. All beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures, the ministry said. The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions. Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE’s northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said. Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have heightened concerns about maritime security and the conflict’s environmental fallout . Ras Al Khaimah, a northern UAE emirate known for its beaches and luxury resorts, is also home to Wynn Resorts’ planned casino resort on Al Marjan Island. The Las Vegas-based operator, which won the UAE’s first commercial gaming license in 2024, said in February it expected the resort to open in the first quarter of 2027. Wynn said in March it had resumed construction after a brief pause, even as the Iran war continued to disrupt businesses across the Middle East. Residents reported unusual odors in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE’s environment ministry said they posed no health risks. The smell remained pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday. UAE authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. REUTERS/Enea Lebrun By Devon Pendleton and Fabiano Maisonnave Oct 22, 2026 (Bloomberg) –To hedge-fund billionaire Louis Bacon, the crystalline waters and densely forested riverways of the Gulf of Chiriqui in western Panama are an ecological oasis. To developer John McKeown, the gulf is a conduit to potential markets for the region’s prized produce and a boon for its economy. Those clashing visions are at the heart of a bitter dispute between the two wealthy Americans, who both say they’re championing Panama’s best interests. The feud centers on a $260 million port McKeown is seeking to develop on the country’s Pacific coast, just south of the city of David. Ocean Pacific Investments, the company McKeown leads, describes the project, Puerto Baru, as Panama’s first “green” port that will help relieve pressure on trading hubs in Panama City and integrate with trade routes to North America and Asia. Chiriqui, with a population of around 500,000, is Panama’s breadbasket, cultivating foods including coffee, papayas and shrimp. The battle has escalated all the way to Panama’s Supreme Court, which is weighing the port’s environmental approval after a group of local nonprofits challenged it. Already, the fight has involved civil and criminal complaints against some of those NGOs. The outcome will dictate the fate of an unspoiled pocket of Panama that’s seen little of the wealth that flows through its high-flying capital. To Bacon, the project poses an unacceptable risk. “I am concerned that the principals behind this project have no experience developing or operating commercial ports, yet they are proposing a major port in one of the most environmentally sensitive areas in Panama,” he wrote in a statement to Bloomberg News. “A simple look at the map would tell you this is not a suitable development site.” Ocean Pacific, for its part, said that it has addressed potential environmental impacts and that the campaign to stop the port may be motivated by personal interests. “If I believed Puerto Baru would cause significant harm to a part of Panama, a country I not only love but call home, I would never have committed myself or my resources to developing this project,” McKeown said in a statement. The site at issue is nested among the serpentine channels that hold a quarter of Panama’s mangrove forests. Mangrove trees and their dense root systems fortify coastlines, shelter sea life and suck up enormous amounts of carbon . Ocean Pacific envisages a 124-hectare (306-acre) commercial port. It would be the biggest private investment in Chiriqui Province’s history, Ocean Pacific says, and the area would benefit not just from an increase in industry but also more tourism, since there will be a dock for leisure vessels. An economic assessment commissioned by the company in 2021 estimated that the project could create upwards of 1,100 jobs. Six Panamanian environmental groups say the facility, and the resulting cargo-ship traffic, would irreversibly damage the local ecosystem through pollution , water churn and blocked sunlight. Juan Carlos Monterrey Gómez, chief executive officer of environmental consultancy VANGLabs and Panama’s former special representative for climate change, said some impact on the local environment from a project of this size is inevitable. (Monterrey isn’t affiliated with any of the groups opposing it.) A spokesman for Ocean Pacific said the company “strongly disagrees” that the port will cause irreparable damage and said potential impacts were “studied extensively and addressed in detail” as part of the environmental review, which was approved two years ago and was comparable, he said, to reviews conducted for US infrastructure projects. The analysis took four years, according to Ocean Pacific, and included a well-attended public hearing. A website for the project describes it as designed to meet “high sustainability standards,” with solar panels for all its power needs and dedicated conservation zones. The spokesman also said the company has always been clear that it is not a port operator itself, and intends to partner with one. Ocean Pacific has continued to work on the port while the court considers the case. But it struck back at the nonprofits, filing criminal complaints against two of them for slander, libel and crimes against the economy. Shortly afterwards, the two nonprofits said that their bank accounts were frozen due to a court order. Unable to pay staff or raise funds, the groups are struggling to stay afloat and the staff say the measures have spooked other charities that might otherwise be speaking out. The case is producing the kind of chill associated with so-called SLAPP lawsuits, which are meant to intimidate critics, said Joana Abrego, former legal manager and now an external consultant for CIAM, one of the affected groups. Ocean Pacific declined to comment on ongoing litigation. One reason that CIAM and the other accused nonprofit, Adopta Bosque, were able to voice such strong opposition in the first place is Louis Bacon. The 70-year-old financier made a fortune through his hedge fund Moore Capital Management and has poured some of it into land and various conservation efforts around the world. He’s the 70th-biggest landowner in the US, according to the Land Report , and has placed 94% of that land under conservation easements, a legal tool that permanently bans future development. The term conservationist suggests quiet stewardship, but that’s not Bacon’s style. He co-founded Waterkeeper Alliance, a nonprofit formerly run by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that aims to enforce environmental laws. Through his nonprofit, the Moore Charitable Foundation, he has often taken an activist approach, collaborating with local advocacy groups to oppose projects near his properties, such as a cement plant in North Carolina. He notably was involved in a bitter yearslong feud with Peter Nygard, the disgraced Canadian fashion mogul, that was tied to their neighboring properties in the Bahamas. The fight over Baru, too, is personal. Bacon owns Islas Secas, an all-inclusive eco-tourism resort that sits on an archipelago about 30 miles southwest of the proposed port, and where nightly rates start at $3,500. He said the port, if built, is far away enough that it won’t directly affect his island, but the dredging and habitat disruption would have cascading consequences. He’s not fighting the project to defend his luxury hotel, he said, and his commitment to Panama won’t change even if the port goes ahead. Bacon described Ocean Pacific’s legal action against the nonprofits as extraordinary. “I’ve never had to support environmental advocates facing criminal penalties simply for raising concerns about a development project,” he said. “Lawfare against whistleblowers is abominable.” Bacon has personally covered Adopta Bosque’s legal costs and also helped fund the broader campaign against the project, which includes an online petition and a website articulating the six nonprofits’ mission, endorsed by nearly four dozen “supportive organizations,” many of which Bacon has funded in the past for their wider work. He paid for an alternative port plan that endorsed moving it about 50 miles west to the city of Puerto Armuelles, and his foundation funded an impact analysis that estimated the port’s environmental toll would come to around $30 million over 20 years. McKeown also has personal ties to Panama. A part-time resident of the country, he said he first became interested in Chiriqui’s potential as a maritime hub while on a deep-sea fishing excursion; the captain had to travel seven hours to resupply because there was no suitable dock. He has experience bridging enterprise and conservation efforts. As president of the closely-held Los Angeles-area energy company, Synergy Oil & Gas, he helped create one of California’s biggest protected wetlands with authorities by agreeing to decommission what had been an active oil field. Before Synergy, McKeown was a real estate broker and owned several container and logistics yards. He said he’s raised money for Puerto Baru from various US individuals, whom he declined to identify. Bacon said he’s expressed his concerns about the project with Panamanian officials personally and through his local foundation, and that he reached out to Ocean Pacific with an offer to help pay for additional scientific analyses and a coastal modeling study but didn’t get a response. An Ocean Pacific spokesman said McKeown exchanged emails with Bacon’s son Trevor and concluded that new analyses would duplicate work that had already been done. McKeown said Puerto Armuelles was too far from the region’s farms to be feasible. Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said in a statement that the ministry is legally “obliged to respect” the environmental approval for Puerto Baru — which a previous administration signed off on — and that it will abide by the Supreme Court’s decision when it comes. He declined to comment on Ocean Pacific’s lawsuits against the NGOs but said the nature of the suits had ministry officials “deeply concerned.” “Panama is a democratic country,” he said. “At the Ministry of Environment we value and promote active, robust citizen participation, as well as contributions from civil society and the scientific community to environmental management.” Panamanian advocates say the port project exposes what they describe as a chasm between Panama’s reputation as a leader on conservation and the environment and its treatment of local nonprofits. “Organizations like ours are on our own. We don’t have institutions that protect us in this situation,” said Abrego. Two environmentalists opposing Puerto Baru declined to speak on the record out of fear for their safety criticizing the state’s stance on a development project. The dissonance isn’t that unusual, said Monterrey, the former climate envoy, given the knotty bureaucratic interests that complicate most countries’ policies. In his view, the port likely wouldn’t deliver what its developers are promising for Panama. “These large projects are usually presented as bringing jobs and development,” he said, “but they often produce social conflict, extract wealth from the communities and send the returns elsewhere.” Whether Ocean Pacific gets the chance to change that narrative is now up to the high court. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: The Trump administration on Friday unveiled its America First Seafood Strategy, outlining plans to strengthen the U.S. commercial fishing industry through regulatory reform, investment in fishing vessels and shoreside infrastructure,...

Join the leading maritime news network Image credit: NOAA Fisheries The Trump administration on Friday unveiled its America First Seafood Strategy, outlining plans to strengthen the U.S. commercial fishing industry through regulatory reform, investment in fishing vessels and shoreside infrastructure, and tougher enforcement against unfair foreign competition. The strategy , announced October 23, builds on President Donald Trump’s April 2025 executive order, Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness , and brings together several federal agencies to expand domestic seafood production, modernize processing capacity, and improve market access for American fishermen. A major focus is rebuilding the infrastructure that supports the nation’s commercial fishing fleet, including shipyards, docks, cold storage facilities, processing plants, and working waterfronts. Federal agencies will work to streamline permitting and reduce barriers to private investment, while making greater use of existing financing programs administered by NOAA, the Department of Agriculture, and the Small Business Administration. NOAA will also review its Fisheries Finance Program and Capital Construction Fund to identify obstacles that discourage fishermen from replacing aging vessels or investing in safer, more efficient American-built fishing boats. “The America First Seafood Strategy ensures that the future of seafood in the United States will be built by American fishermen, American workers, and American industry—not by foreign imports,” said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. The initiative comes as the administration pursues a broader effort to rebuild America’s maritime industrial base, including domestic shipbuilding capacity and the U.S.-flagged fleet. Beyond infrastructure, the strategy calls for changes to federal fisheries management aimed at increasing sustainable harvests and reducing regulatory costs. NOAA will work with regional fishery management councils and industry representatives to ensure catch limits reflect the best available science, restore access to productive fishing grounds where supported by data, and eliminate compliance requirements that do not contribute to conservation goals. The administration also plans to strengthen the position of American seafood in domestic markets. A proposed voluntary “U.S.-Caught Seafood” designation would help consumers identify products harvested by American fishermen aboard U.S.-flagged vessels operating under U.S. fisheries management. The Food and Drug Administration issued draft guidance Friday outlining how companies could use U.S.-origin statements and labeling. Federal agencies will also seek to expand purchases of American seafood through government procurement programs and launch a nationwide “Eat American Seafood” campaign. On the trade front, the strategy calls for stronger enforcement against illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, seafood fraud, and mislabeling. NOAA plans to improve its Seafood Import Monitoring Program, using advanced technology and more targeted inspections to identify high-risk imports. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative will also work with other agencies to address unfair foreign trade practices and improve access to overseas markets for American seafood exporters. Marine aquaculture is another priority, with federal agencies expected to establish clearer permitting standards for operations in federal waters. Notably, the strategy does not announce new federal spending. Instead, it relies on existing programs and statutory authorities, with an emphasis on regulatory changes, interagency coordination, and attracting private investment. NOAA said progress will be measured through increases in domestic seafood production and processing, private capital investment, American jobs supported, and reduced dependence on foreign supply chains. The broader goal is to keep more of the economic value of American seafood in the United States, from vessels harvesting fish offshore to the shipyards, processors, and waterfront businesses that support the industry.
